contract_plain_english: For the N-component output-error vector, the largest component magnitude is at most sqrt(N) times the paper's normalized RMS error. This exact algebraic conversion is what turns Theorem 1(a)'s RMS estimate into Theorem 1(b)'s maximum-error estimate. (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: proof of Theorem 1(b))

source_evidence.observation: The exact output is an N-entry complex Fourier transform, and the paper defines ||z||_RMS = ((sum_k |z(k)|^2)/N)^(1/2) and ||z||_infinity = max_k |z(k)|.
For a floating-point FFT of order N=N_1...N_M, Theorem 1 states an RMS relative-error bound with constant K(N,gamma) and a maximum-error bound containing the additional factor sqrt(N).

source_evidence.observation: After defining e(j)=fl(y(j))-y(j), the paper states max_i |e(i)|^2 <= sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|e(j)|^2 and consequently max_i |e(i)| <= sqrt(N)||e||_RMS; substituting Theorem 1(a) completes part (b).

statement.algorithm_linkage: The conversion applies to the output error of the paper's one-dimensional mixed-radix floating-point FFT. The matrix factorization is stated to cover both Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey forms, with different diagonal factors; the norm conversion itself is algorithm-independent. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equation (2.2) and the paragraph following it; PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: proof of Theorem 1(b))
binders: N is the number of Fourier output components, indexed from 0 through N-1, and e(j):=fl(y(j))-y(j) is the corresponding complex output-error component. (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: proof of Theorem 1(b), definition of e(j))
In the enclosing theorem, y=Tx and the floating-point FFT order factors as N=N_1N_2...N_M. (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1)
conclusions: max_i |e(i)|^2 <= sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|e(j)|^2. (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: first unnumbered display in the proof of Theorem 1(b))
max_i |e(i)| <= sqrt(N)||e||_RMS. (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: second unnumbered display in the proof of Theorem 1(b))

Using Theorem 1(a), the conversion yields ||fl(y)-y||_infinity/||y||_RMS < sqrt(N)K(N,gamma)epsilon + O(epsilon^2), which is Theorem 1(b). (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1(a)-(b); PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: closing sentence of the proof of part (b))
constants_and_indexing: Both sums and maxima range over the N output indices 0,...,N-1; the source writes j for the sum and i for the maximum. (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: proof of Theorem 1(b))
The factor is exactly sqrt(N), with no offset, radix-dependent constant, or replacement by N. (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: second unnumbered display)

In the enclosing theorem K(N,gamma)=sum_{l=1}^M alpha(N_l)+(M-1)(3+2gamma), where alpha(2)=sqrt(2), alpha(4)=5, and alpha(q)=2sqrt(q)(q+gamma) otherwise. (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: definition of K and alpha in Theorem 1)
definitions_and_conventions: ||e||_RMS=((sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|e(j)|^2)/N)^(1/2), while ||e||_infinity=max_i |e(i)|. (PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: RMS and infinity-norm definitions)
fl(y) denotes the floating-point representation or computed result corresponding to the exact Fourier output y. (PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: paragraph following equation (1.1))
error_notions: e is absolute componentwise output error, and max_i |e(i)| is the maximum absolute output error. (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: definition of e(j) and following displays)
The enclosing theorem normalizes both RMS and maximum output errors by the exact output RMS value ||y||_RMS. (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1(a)-(b))

Theorem 1(a) supplies the RMS roundoff bound; the selected passage is the deterministic conversion used to prove Theorem 1(b), rather than a separate probabilistic estimate. (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1; PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: proof of part (b))
norms: The RMS norm is the Euclidean norm divided by sqrt(N), not the unnormalized Euclidean norm. (PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: RMS definition)

The maximum norm is max over component magnitudes, and the selected conclusion is ||e||_infinity <= sqrt(N)||e||_RMS. (PDF p. 1, printed p. 757, anchor: infinity-norm definition; PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: second unnumbered display)
numerical_model: The enclosing theorem uses fl(a+b)=a(1+theta epsilon)+b(1+theta epsilon) and fl(ab)=ab(1+theta epsilon), with each theta in [-1,1] and epsilon computer-dependent. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2))

It separately models trigonometric computation by fl(sin(fl(a)))=sin(a)+gamma theta epsilon and fl(cos(fl(a)))=cos(a)+gamma theta epsilon, with gamma>=0 independent of the input data. (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute sine-and-cosine error model)
The exact max-versus-RMS conversion introduces no epsilon, gamma, or higher-order approximation. (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: two unnumbered displays in the proof of Theorem 1(b))

The squared inequality and its square-root consequence are both part of the selected passage and both use non-strict <=. (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: two unnumbered displays)
